definition: In machine learning, instance-based learning (sometimes called memory-based learning) is a family of learning algorithms that compare new problem instances with instances seen in training, which have been stored in memory.
details: Because computation is postponed until a new instance is observed, these algorithms are sometimes referred to as "lazy."

explainer.lead: A family of learning algorithms that compare new problem instances with training instances kept in memory. It matters because computation is postponed until a new instance arrives, making these algorithms lazy.

tiers.eli5: Like solving a new problem by flipping back to similar examples you kept in a notebook instead of learning a rule up front.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers store training instances and compare new inputs against them at prediction time. A pitfall is that memory and query cost grow with the stored data.
tiers.paperLevel: Algorithms that compare new problem instances with stored training instances; computation is postponed until a new instance is observed, hence lazy.

explainer.example: A new patient record is classified by comparing it to stored past records rather than applying a pre-learned model.
